newsitem.title: USA: Rising revenues may help NYC avoid big FY '97 cuts.
newsitem.headline: Rising revenues may help NYC avoid big FY '97 cuts.

text.p: New York City, which faces up to a $2 billion budget gap in the 1998 fiscal year, might not have to make big cuts this autumn because revenues have been surprisingly strong, city and state sources said on Friday.
"What we're hearing is that they do not anticipate a major revision at this time," said one of the city sources, who declined to be named.

"The 1997 fiscal year is pretty well shored up," the source added, explaining that the year should get at least some benefit from the Giuliani Administration's decision to ask city agencies to come up with $500 million of savings.
The latest round of cuts, which aim to narrow future budget gaps, comes on the heels of the $1.1 billion that was slashed from agency budgets in the current budget.

But even with these reductions and a surge in revenues, which ran about $183 million above the City Council's forecast in the first fiscal quarter, New York City probably cannot avoid making harsher decisions by January, the sources said.

"The rise in revenues will never be enough to bail Mayor Rudolph Giuliani out. He's got a $2 billion problem in 1998," said one of the sources, who requested anonymity. New York City projects a smaller budget gap of $1.7 billion than some of the fiscal monitors.
Giuliani's spokesman was not immediately available to comment.
Looming budget gaps likely will force New York City to make some tough decisions, which are expected to be announced in January, when its mid-year budget adjustment is due.
"Even if revenues pick up a little bit, Giuliani still has to do something on the expenditure side," said another source, who also declined to be named.

One advantage of holding off on such decisions is that Gov. George Pataki has said he will unveil his welfare bill over the next several weeks, adding he aims to call a special legislative session to take up the bill in December.

The state and city already have clashed over how generous the state program, which has to be reshaped to meet stiff, new federal curbs, should be. While Pataki wants to preserve benefits like Medicaid for legal immigrants, Giuliani has sued the federal government to protect the rights of 400,000 illegal aliens who use public hospitals and schools.

Delaying the first budget modification, which first was scheduled for October 24, until a week or two after the November 5 polls, will help keep the issue of cost cuts out of the public's eye, the sources said. They added it also gives the city more time to review revenues.

How quickly the Giuliani Administration puts the $500 million of cuts in place will be one the most closely scrutinized issues. While there was speculation the reductions will include trimming the approximately 200,000 workers who are paid by the city, the sources said such efforts likely would focus on attrition or early retirement.
Giuliani agreed there would be no layoffs with the city's unions until June 1998 and in any case, they might provoke too much controversy in an election year.
New York City anticipated approximately 4,000 workers would take an early retirement package that ended on Friday.

One of the most positive developments is the fatter tax collections, as the economic rebound and strong financial markets have raised general corporate tax revenues by 17.2 percent in the first fiscal quarter, a financial source said. This is as much $80 million over a year-ago.

New York City collected an extra $38 million in sales tax revenues, which rose 5.8 percent, the source said. The city, which claims the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey owes it over $543 million in back rent for its airports, so far has gotten more than it expected in the 1996 calender year, though it might not get the full $70 million it wants.

A spokesman for the Authority said it has paid the city about $40 million in rent so far this year, adding that while it expects pay a total of $48 million, a sharp rise from last year's $17 million, the increase is due to better management.
"Generousity had nothing to do with it," he said.
--U.S. Municipal Desk, 212-859-1654
